title: Where Training-Compute Growth Comes From
question: How much training-compute growth came from faster accelerators versus a larger, longer-running fleet?
scope: These are fitted historical trends with estimated run data. A trend fit is not a forecast or a causal attribution to hardware alone.

steps.title: Read the historical trend
steps.description: Panel (a) places notable runs by publication date and training FLOPs on a logarithmic axis. The domain colors and dashed least-squares fit summarize substantial variation between individual runs.

steps.title: Separate fleet size from total compute
steps.description: Panel (b) gives annual growth factors for the reporting subset. Accelerator count is one multiplicative contributor to compute growth; its bar is not the entire compute increase.

steps.title: Account for runtime and delivered rate
steps.description: Training duration and delivered rate per accelerator supply the remaining factors. Delivered rate includes both hardware speed and utilization; logarithmic bar lengths make multiplicative growth contributions comparable.

title: The scale discontinuity
question: What changes when one machine becomes a synchronized fleet?
scope: The fleet panel depicts tightly coupled work; independent serving requests need not wait at the same barrier.

steps.title: Start at the local memory wall
steps.description: The single-machine panel places HBM below its accelerators. Every accelerator-memory link crosses the red memory wall; there are no peer nodes to wait for.

steps.title: Cross the fleet network
steps.description: The fleet connects multiple nodes through the amber network fabric. This shared communication path introduces a network wall beyond each node’s local memory wall.

steps.title: Place and recover the job
steps.description: Scheduler and recovery sit above the node group. Coordination must manage placement and failures as well as the compute and communication substrates.

steps.title: Identify fleet-wide waiting
steps.description: One node is failed and another slow while healthy nodes are labeled waiting. A required participant can hold up synchronized progress; more accelerators alone do not remove that dependency.

title: Retryable tasks vs. shared training steps
question: Why does a slow worker affect synchronous training differently from a retryable map task?
scope: These are illustrative critical paths. MapReduce still has downstream dependencies; synchronous-training penalties depend on overlap.

steps.title: Finish independent map work
steps.description: Map 1 and Map 2 emit their own outputs and finish. They do not wait for Map 3 to retry.

steps.title: Retry the missing contribution
steps.description: Only Map 3 is re-run after its failure. Its missing output delays the reduce work that depends on it.

steps.title: Wait for every required gradient
steps.description: Workers 0 and 1 finish compute before slow Worker 2. Their gray waiting segments end only when the AllReduce can collect all required contributions.

steps.title: Advance one shared step
steps.description: The update follows the collective. Consistent shared progress is why local retry techniques need additional coordination in synchronous training.

title: Data scaling regimes
question: When does collecting more data produce predictable returns and when does it produce little gain?
scope: The three regimes are schematic, without measured boundaries. An observed plateau can also reflect limited coverage, insufficient model capacity, or incomplete optimization; it does not prove an irreducible floor.

steps.title: Recognize the best-guess regime
steps.description: The curve begins near Best Guess Error and is labeled little gain. The figure does not assume every new data point yields the same improvement.

steps.title: Read the predictable-return regime
steps.description: In the power-law region, the line descends at approximately constant slope on log axes. Equal proportional increases in data follow a regular reduction pattern within this regime.

steps.title: Identify a limit data alone cannot remove
steps.description: The curve flattens at Irreducible Error. The hatched region below the floor is excluded by this schematic assumption, so extrapolating the middle slope indefinitely would be misleading.

title: The reliability collapse
question: Why can very reliable nodes still yield poor simultaneous availability for a large job?
scope: The curves assume independent node availability and an unreplicated job requiring every node. They do not model recovery or actual useful training goodput.

steps.title: Read the job’s joint requirement
steps.description: The horizontal axis is required job size on a log scale; the vertical axis is simultaneous all-node availability. Requiring every node compounds individual unavailability.

steps.title: Follow the larger required set
steps.description: The blue 99.9%-per-node curve reaches 36.8% at 1,000 nodes and approaches the bottom by 10,000. Good individual availability does not transfer unchanged to the all-node event.

steps.title: Postpone rather than remove the problem
steps.description: The green curve reaches the same 36.8% at 10,000 required nodes. The extra nine shifts the collapse to a larger job under this model; resilience still needs system-level mechanisms.

title: End-to-end inference pipeline
question: Which parts of a language-model request spend the first-token and per-token latency budgets?
scope: One request is traced. Segment widths are illustrative, and the CPU/GPU split does not quantify achieved latency.

steps.title: Prepare the request
steps.description: The load balancer routes and admits the request, then the CPU tokenizer creates token IDs. These steps spend latency before GPU prefill starts.

steps.title: Process the whole prompt
steps.description: Prefill processes the prompt in one pass and writes keys and values to the KV cache in HBM. This stored state is reused during generation.

steps.title: Generate one token at a time
steps.description: Decode reads and appends the KV cache on successive steps. Generated token IDs return to CPU detokenization and the response stream.

steps.title: Separate TTFT from token pacing
steps.description: Time to first token includes routing, preprocessing, and prefill. The decode segment contains per-token steps; CPU work and routing are serving-tax costs outside GPU compute.

review_notes: Inspected canonical PNG from the fresh rendered chapter using /tmp/mlsys-figure-art/index.json, checked original geometry and local source context. Guided original-art annotation, not a numerical simulation.

title: Batching strategies compared
question: How does batch formation trade waiting against shared GPU passes?
scope: This is an illustrative arrival timeline. Formation delay is separate from waiting for an occupied worker.

steps.title: Run four individual passes
steps.description: Each request gets a separate GPU forward pass. Later requests wait while earlier passes occupy the worker.

steps.title: Wait for the full batch
steps.description: The batch-full line dispatches all four requests together. Early arrivals wait longest, and shorter requests incur hatched padding to match the longest request.

steps.title: Close a short formation window
steps.description: The two window-closing lines dispatch two requests at a time. In this example, intentional formation delay is bounded while each pass serves more than one request.

title: Decode inherits the bandwidth deficit
question: Why does rising peak compute not eliminate the decode bandwidth constraint?
scope: The hardware ratios are relative to V100 and use the chapter’s selected specifications. Peak ratios are not achieved application speedups.

steps.title: Normalize both resources
steps.description: Both series begin at the V100 reference and grow toward newer devices. The y-axis measures relative growth, not absolute FLOPs or bytes per second.

steps.title: Compare compute with bandwidth growth
steps.description: The black peak-compute series rises faster than the purple memory-bandwidth series. The B200 endpoint labels show a larger compute multiplier than bandwidth multiplier.

steps.title: Relate the gap to decode
steps.description: The shaded gap is the bandwidth deficit. Decode that repeatedly reads model state can remain constrained by data delivery even as arithmetic capacity grows; the plot alone does not quantify its runtime.

title: Throughput versus Interactivity in Measured LLM Serving
question: How does the measured throughput frontier change when each user needs faster token delivery?
scope: Points are benchmark observations for the source workload and system configurations. Frontiers do not establish isolated hardware causality or predict arbitrary deployments.

steps.title: Keep aggregate rate separate from user rate
steps.description: The x-axis is output tokens per second per user, or inverse TPOT; the log y-axis is output tokens per second per GPU. The dashed line marks the 50-token/s/user reference.

steps.title: Observe batching’s throughput side
steps.description: The upper-left frontier points combine high aggregate output with lower user interactivity. These are observed operating points rather than an assertion that maximizing batch size always wins.

steps.title: Compare valid operating points
steps.description: The curves generally fall as per-user token rate rises. The legend distinguishes system configurations; a serving choice must satisfy user pacing as well as aggregate throughput.

title: Static vs. continuous batching
question: What happens to a decode slot when its request finishes?
scope: The illustrated iterations show slot utilization, not measured throughput or a guarantee that prefill has zero cost.

steps.title: Leave completed slots idle
steps.description: In static batching, R1, R3, and R4 finish before R2. Their subsequent hatched cells stay idle until the batch ends.

steps.title: Admit waiting requests into freed slots
steps.description: Continuous batching places R5, R6, and R7 into freed slots. Dark cells identify their prefill steps before later decode cells.

steps.title: Compare the same iteration window
steps.description: The panels report 20 of 32 busy slots for static batching and 32 of 32 for continuous batching. These totals describe the drawn schedule, not every workload.

title: Feature-parallel batching pipeline
question: How does one recommendation request combine sharded feature lookups?
scope: Highlighted embedding rows are schematic lookups; this diagram does not specify measured communication or ranking latency.

steps.title: Route features by type
steps.description: The request reaches Feature split, which separates user, item, and context features. Each feature type can then address its embedding shards.

steps.title: Fetch the needed rows
steps.description: User, item, and context tables are distributed across shard 0 and shard 1. Dark rows identify the entries needed by this request, rather than scanning every row.

steps.title: Reassemble inputs for dense scoring
steps.description: Orange gather paths concatenate the retrieved embeddings into U, I, and C. The dense MLP ranking head consumes that assembled representation to produce ranked output.

title: The KV cache wall
question: How do sequence length and concurrency compete for a fixed HBM budget?
scope: This is the chapter’s idealized 35-GB weight-plus-KV capacity model under a decimal 80-GB budget. Quantization metadata, runtime buffers, and other allocations make its capacity boundary optimistic; it does not predict achieved bandwidth.

steps.title: Reserve memory before caching tokens
steps.description: The blue base is Model weights (35 GB), independent of sequence length in this scenario. It consumes capacity before any request’s growing KV state.

steps.title: Add cache growth for active sequences
steps.description: The batch-1, batch-2, batch-4, and batch-8 lines rise as sequence length grows. More concurrent sequences increase KV growth and use the remaining HBM sooner.

steps.title: Locate capacity-limited sequence lengths
steps.description: The red dashed HBM capacity line meets larger batches at shorter lengths. The region above it is infeasible under the stated capacity assumptions, regardless of spare arithmetic throughput.

title: Prefix caching via block sharing
question: Which KV blocks can two requests reuse without sharing their distinct suffixes?
scope: Reuse requires identical token prefixes and compatible model computation, adapters, and other state-affecting inputs, with authorized tenant sharing. Matching visible text alone is insufficient.

steps.title: Identify the reusable prefix
steps.description: Request A’s green logical pages P0 through P5 form the shared prefix. The ellipsis omits intermediate pages without changing the prefix boundary.

steps.title: Map both requests to one copy
steps.description: Both requests’ green prefix pages point to B0 through B5 in GPU HBM. Logical page identity is separate from physical block ownership and reuse.

steps.title: Keep suffix state distinct
steps.description: Suffix A maps to B10 and B11, while suffix B maps to B12 through B14. Newly diverging tokens require distinct state even when earlier prefix blocks are shared.

title: Disaggregated Serving Architecture
question: Why separate prefill and decode pools, and what state crosses between them?
scope: The source’s long-prompt, small-decode-batch regime labels prefill compute-bound and decode bandwidth-bound. Other batch or context sizes can change the bottleneck; transfers and pool queueing still add latency.

steps.title: Complete the prompt pass
steps.description: The prefill pool runs whole-prompt passes and sets time to first token. Its capacity is sized for prompt tokens per second.

steps.title: Transfer the request state
steps.description: The amber KV cache path moves prompt-derived state by RDMA to the decode pool. Disaggregation adds this transfer rather than eliminating the cache.

steps.title: Sustain token-by-token output
steps.description: The decode pool performs repeated one-token steps and sets time per output token. Its capacity is sized for output tokens per second.

title: Tensor parallelism for inference
question: Where do two tensor-parallel GPUs need to exchange partial results?
scope: This is the printed two-GPU decomposition; it is not a claim that every tensor-parallel implementation uses identical collective placement.

steps.title: Compute different attention heads
steps.description: GPU 0 holds the first half of the attention heads and GPU 1 the second half. Each produces a partial output from its local share.

steps.title: Combine attention contributions
steps.description: The first amber AllReduce combines the attention partial outputs across the NVLink path before the feed-forward block.

steps.title: Keep the intermediate local
steps.description: Column slices of W1 produce activations locally. The diagram marks no communication between W1 and row slices of W2; each GPU then produces a partial sum.

steps.title: Finish the shared layer output
steps.description: The second AllReduce combines W2 partial sums. Only after this exchange does the next layer receive the completed output.

title: Pipeline parallelism bubbles
question: How can several independent requests fill a pipeline that one request cannot?
scope: Time cells are illustrative stage slots; this diagram does not model unequal stage times or the pipeline drain.

steps.title: Follow one request’s dependencies
steps.description: One request passes through Stage 0 to Stage 3 in order. Activations cross GPUs; the later stage cannot process that request before its predecessor finishes.

steps.title: Account for initial idle slots
steps.description: In the multi-request timeline, lower GPUs initially show hatched fill bubbles. They are idle because no earlier stage has supplied activations yet.

steps.title: Overlap different requests
steps.description: Once filled, each GPU works on a different request in the same time slot. This raises aggregate utilization while each individual request still traverses all stages.

title: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing
question: How does top-2 expert routing create communication around sparse computation?
scope: The four tokens and three experts are a schematic assignment; routing does not guarantee balanced expert load.

steps.title: Choose experts per token
steps.description: The gate selects two experts for each token. This selection changes which devices must receive that token’s activations.

steps.title: Dispatch to selected expert devices
steps.description: AllToAll dispatch sends token copies to the chosen experts. Token t1 appears at Expert A and Expert B; the other shown assignments need not be equally distributed.

steps.title: Combine selected expert outputs
steps.description: AllToAll gather returns the expert outputs. The weighted sum uses the gate weights to form one output for each token; selecting fewer experts does not remove communication.

title: Embedding sharding strategies
question: What does an embedding lookup transfer under each sharding layout?
scope: The printed AllToAll and AllGather are realizations of these layouts, not collectives mandated by placement alone. A runtime can instead use shard RPCs; hot-row replication consumes extra capacity.

steps.title: Split IDs across servers
steps.description: Row-wise sharding gives each server whole vectors for some IDs. AllToAll routes lookups and whole vectors to the servers that own them.

steps.title: Split each vector’s dimensions
steps.description: Column-wise sharding places a slice of every vector on each server. AllGather assembles the slices needed to recover a complete embedding.

steps.title: Replicate hot rows and shard the tail
steps.description: The hybrid panel duplicates hot rows while distributing cold rows. The printed AllToAll applies to the cold tail; the replicated hot portion consumes extra storage.

review_notes: Inspected canonical PNG from the fresh rendered chapter using /tmp/mlsys-figure-art/index.json, checked original geometry and local source context. Guided original-art annotation, not a numerical simulation.

title: Horizontal scaling with shard groups
question: Why do more shard groups increase aggregate serving capacity without replacing tensor-parallel communication?
scope: One group is one model replica with TP=8 in this schematic. More groups do not inherently reduce one request’s latency.

steps.title: Choose a replica group
steps.description: The load balancer sends each request to a shard group using a policy such as round-robin, two-choice, or session affinity.

steps.title: Communicate within the selected replica

title: Circuit breaker states
question: How does a circuit breaker protect a failing dependency and decide when to retry?
scope: Transitions describe policy states, not fixed timing or a universal error threshold.

steps.title: Allow normal traffic
steps.description: Closed forwards ordinary requests to the dependency. Errors, timeouts, or latency that exceed the configured threshold move the breaker to Open.

steps.title: Fail fast while the dependency recovers
steps.description: Open rejects requests rather than continuing to load the dependency. A timeout must elapse before the breaker permits limited probes.

steps.title: Probe with bounded traffic
steps.description: Half-open limits probes. A successful probe returns to Closed; a failed probe sends the breaker back to Open instead of immediately restoring full traffic.

title: Spot-aware traffic distribution
question: How does SLO-aware routing use spot capacity without treating it as always available?
scope: The 70/30 split is the printed scenario, not a recommended universal allocation. Spot capacity can be reclaimed.

steps.title: Classify each request’s contract
steps.description: Requests carry an SLO class. The gateway classifies the contract, watches preemption notices, and coordinates draining.

steps.title: Reserve stable capacity for critical work
steps.description: The SLO-critical path reaches Workers 0–2 in the on-demand pool. This scenario avoids spot reclamation on that pool.

steps.title: Drain reclaimable capacity
steps.description: Best-effort work reaches the spot pool. Worker 5 is draining after an eviction notice, so new work must respect its changing readiness instead of treating all workers as interchangeable.

title: Serving deployment stack
question: How does the serving stack spend latency before and during GPU generation?
scope: These are stated tier budgets, not measurements; bar length is proportional to the logarithm of budget.

steps.title: Authorize before edge reuse

steps.title: Enforce and route the request

steps.title: Run prefill and decode
steps.description: The GPU worker runs prefill then decode and streams tokens back. The autoscaler uses queue depth and KV usage to manage workers, while readiness limits how quickly extra capacity can help.

title: Ranking cascade architecture
question: Why spend more model work on fewer recommendation candidates?
scope: Candidate counts and latency budgets are the printed schematic; band width follows log candidate count rather than a linear count.

steps.title: Filter a very large candidate pool
steps.description: Lexical and ANN retrieval reduces 1,000,000 candidates to 10,000 under the smallest shown latency budget. It preserves a tractable pool for later models.

steps.title: Reserve heavier scoring for survivors
steps.description: First-stage ranking reduces 10,000 to 1,000; second-stage scoring reduces 1,000 to 100. The latency budget increases as the candidate pool shrinks.

steps.title: Apply the most expensive comparison selectively
steps.description: The cross-attention transformer reranks 100 candidates down to 10 under the largest shown budget. Early filtering controls how many candidates incur this final cost. A relevant candidate discarded upstream cannot be recovered by the final ranker, so filtering also creates a recall constraint.

title: Production Responsible AI Architecture
question: Which governance checks can run without blocking every inference response?
scope: The architecture separates synchronous service from asynchronous review; monitoring by itself does not authorize a model update.

steps.title: Keep the serving path bounded
steps.description: Request, access control and minimization, inference, and response sit inside the serving SLO. They are the synchronous path for one decision.

steps.title: Separate immediate records from later labels
steps.description: Inference emits bounded evidence records. Older decisions have known outcomes; recent decisions remain pending, so label-dependent error metrics cannot yet include them.

steps.title: Compute only metrics the evidence supports
steps.description: Explanations and parity metrics consume decision evidence. Error-rate metrics additionally require matched outcomes; these governance computations occur asynchronously.

steps.title: Require an authorized update
steps.description: The named owner’s release gate mediates the dashed approved-update path back to inference. A detected issue supplies evidence for review, not automatic permission to deploy.

title: Privacy Boundaries in Federated Training
question: Which privacy protection applies before aggregation and which applies to the public release?

steps.title: Keep raw records on clients

steps.title: Protect individual contributions during combination
steps.description: Masked update bars combine at the sum node inside Secure aggregation. Protection depends on the protocol’s bounded-collusion and dropout assumptions.

steps.title: Account for released information
steps.description: The trusted curator adds calibrated noise to the aggregate and tracks budget spent per release. Only the released model crosses the public boundary; repeated releases must be accounted for.

title: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) Alignment Pipeline

steps.title: Start from a supervised policy

steps.title: Learn a proxy for preferences

steps.title: Constrain the policy update

steps.title: Follow the data back to the policy
steps.description: Clicks are logged as training data for the next model. This closes a possible reinforcing loop; establishing harm requires evidence about the deployed policy and the user-value criterion.

title: Bias Amplification Feedback Loop
question: Where can interventions interrupt a possible bias-reinforcement loop?
scope: The edges describe a possible reinforcing mechanism; they do not guarantee that each retraining round increases disparity.

steps.title: Inspect training and in-processing
steps.description: Biased training data trains the model. The in-processing box points to the training arc, locating fairness constraints during model fitting.

steps.title: Inspect decisions and post-processing
steps.description: Biased model predictions can produce disparate outcomes. Post-processing threshold calibration intervenes on this decision-to-outcome arc rather than rewriting past training data.

steps.title: Audit what returns as training data
steps.description: Outcomes create new data that can reinforce the original bias. Pre-processing audit and reweighting cut the feeds-into arc before the next training dataset is formed.
